target: Battlefield chronicle #0 "Erebuni Rise" (era 0: Assyrian Invasion, 8th century BC)

claims.quote: In 782 BC
claims.finding: 782 BC is the conventional date. It is the one used for Yerevan's official anniversaries (2,750th in 1968, 2,800th on 21 October 2018) and given by most reference works. The Erebuni stone itself carries no date. The year comes from placing the founding in Argishti I's fifth regnal year, so it depends on when you start his reign: 786 to 764 BC in the Soviet-era chronology (Melikishvili, Arutyunyan), or c. 785/780 to 756 BC in Salvini's. Variants: Encyclopaedia Iranica ('Erevan') puts it in 'the fifth regnal year of Argišti, ca. 780 B.C.E.', Britannica's Yerevan entry gives 783 BC, and Britannica's Erebuni entry says only 'first quarter of the 8th century BC'. Keeping 782 BC is defensible as the consensus convention.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Erevan' (iranicaonline.org/articles/erevan-1); Britannica, 'Erebuni' and 'Yerevan'; Wikipedia, 'Erebuni Fortress', 'Argishti I', 'Etiuni'; Armenian Weekly, 'Yerevan celebrates 2800 years' (1 Nov 2018); AGBU 'Yerevan 2800'

claims.quote: king Argishti I of Urartu raised the fortress of Erebuni on Arin Berd hill
claims.finding: Argishti I, son of Menua, built Erebuni on the Arin Berd mound at the south-eastern edge of modern Yerevan. The founding inscription says he 'built this mighty stronghold and proclaimed it Erebuni'. It was the first Urartian fortress north of the Araxes, and Argishtikhinili followed in 776 BC.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Erevan'; Britannica, 'Erebuni'; World History Encyclopedia (J. B. Wiener), 'Erebuni'; Wikipedia, 'Erebuni Fortress'

claims.quote: settled 6,600 warriors there
claims.finding: The figure is not in the Erebuni stone. It comes from Argishti I's annals carved at Van (the Khorkhor chamber at Tushpa). They record 6,600 soldiers or warriors of the lands of Hate (Hatti, the Neo-Hittite region around Melid) and Tsupani (Sophene) settled at Erebuni. These men were deported prisoners of war brought in to people the new town. They were not an Urartian garrison, so the original's 'settled 6,600 warriors' misleads by leaving that out. Iranica names only Supa/Sophene. Most other accounts give both Hatti and Tsupani. Rewritten as 'his annals at Van record 6,600 captive warriors from Hatti and Tsupani settled there'.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Erevan' (annals at Van, 6,600 warriors from Supa); Wikipedia, 'Argishti I' and 'Erebuni Fortress' (6,600 prisoners of war from Hatti and Supani); World History Encyclopedia, 'Erebuni' (Tushpa inscription, 6,600 prisoners of war from Khate and Tsupani)

claims.quote: the founding inscription survives in cuneiform
claims.finding: A Urartian cuneiform inscription was found on Arin Berd in September/autumn 1950 by K. Hovhannisyan's expedition. Two further identical copies were later found in the citadel. Iranica and Israelyan treat it as the identification document, the 'birth certificate', linking Erebuni to Yerevan.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Erevan'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Erebuni'; Wikipedia, 'Erebuni Fortress'

claims.quote: making Yerevan one of the world's oldest living cities
claims.finding: That Yerevan's name comes from Erebuni is the accepted view, and Iranica says modern Erevan 'can be said to continue both the name and the history of Erebuni'. Continuous habitation is a different matter. Erebuni lost its importance after Teishebaini was founded in the 7th century BC. After an Achaemenid-period phase, the city is not documented again until a 607 AD letter in the Book of Letters and Sebeos's 7th-century 'Erevan'. 'Oldest continuously inhabited city' is a popular boast, not a demonstrated fact. Rewritten as 'Yerevan, named for Erebuni, counts its birth from it', which is true: the official anniversaries are dated from the stone.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Erevan'; Wikipedia, 'History of Yerevan' (607 Book of Letters, Sebeos); Armenian Weekly 2018

claims.quote: older than Rome
claims.finding: This holds only against Rome's legendary founding date of 21 April 753 BC, which Varro fixed in the 1st century BC. Archaeology places huts on the Palatine from the 10th century BC, so the settlement at Rome is older than Erebuni. Rewritten as 'decades before Rome's legendary founding' (782 against 753 BC, a gap of 29 years).
claims.sources: Wikipedia, 'Founding of Rome'; History Today, 'The Foundation of Rome'; Smithsonian, 'Ancient walls show Rome older than legend'

claims.quote: From these walls the garrison watched the Ararat plain against Assyria and the steppe tribes.
claims.finding: Assyria lay far to the south, beyond Lake Van and Tushpa, and no Assyrian army is recorded anywhere near Erebuni. Argishti's Assyrian wars against Shalmaneser IV and the turtan Shamshi-ilu took place on Urartu's southern fronts. Steppe peoples are anachronistic for 782 BC: the Cimmerians first appear in Assyrian intelligence letters of c. 714 BC (under Sargon II), and the Scythians later still. Erebuni was built as a northern stronghold on newly conquered land. In the year of the founding, Argishti campaigned against Etiuni and Qihuni, north-east of the Ararat valley. The inscription says it was raised for the might of Biainili and the terror of enemy lands, and Sarduri II and Rusa I later used it as a base for conquests to the north and around Lake Sevan. Rewritten as 'From these walls Urartu held the Ararat plain and struck north toward Etiuni and Lake Sevan.'
claims.sources: Wikipedia, 'Etiuni' (782 BC campaigns against Etiuni and Kekhuni/Qihuni; 'four kings of Uduri-Etiuni' on Lake Sevan); World History Encyclopedia, 'Erebuni' (Sarduri II and Rusa I staging campaigns north); Wikipedia, 'Cimmerians' (first mention 714 BC, Sennacherib's letters to Sargon II); Wikipedia, 'Shalmaneser IV', 'Shamshi-ilu'

claims.quote: twenty-nine centuries are counting on you
claims.finding: From 782 BC to 2026 AD is 2,807 years (there is no year 0), which is just over 28 centuries. Even counting from today's date in 2026 it does not reach 29. Changed to 'twenty-eight centuries'. The em dash was replaced with a colon.
claims.sources: Arithmetic from the 782 BC date (Iranica, Britannica, Yerevan 2800 jubilee of 2018 = 2,800 years)

claims.quote: The newborn fortress of Argishti on Arin Berd.
claims.finding: The tag is accurate: Erebuni was Argishti I's new foundation on Arin Berd. Kept verbatim (46 characters).
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Erevan'; Britannica, 'Erebuni'

revised.name: Erebuni Rise
revised.tag: The newborn fortress of Argishti on Arin Berd.
revised.history: In 782 BC king Argishti I of Urartu raised the fortress of Erebuni on Arin Berd hill; his annals at Van record 6,600 captive warriors from Hatti and Tsupani settled there. The founding inscription survives in cuneiform, and Yerevan, named for Erebuni, counts its birth from it, decades before Rome's legendary founding. From these walls Urartu held the Ararat plain and struck north toward Etiuni and Lake Sevan. Defend the young city: twenty-eight centuries are counting on you.

rosterFit:
The era roster fits this date and place poorly. No battle or siege at Erebuni is recorded between 782 and 760 BC. Its real foes were the Etiuni confederation and the Uduri-Etiuni kings of the Lake Sevan basin to the north. Assyria fought Argishti I in the same years, but only on Urartu's southern fronts.

Unit by unit:
(1) BOSS 'Sargon, King of Assyria' is anachronistic. Sargon II reigned 722 to 705 BC, beginning about 60 years after Erebuni was founded, and his 714 BC campaign struck Rusa I around Lake Urmia and Musasir, not Erebuni. In Argishti's time the Assyrian king was Shalmaneser IV (r. 783 to 773 BC; the eponym list records campaigns 'to Urartu' in 781 to 776 BC). The real commander against Urartu was the turtan Shamshi-ilu, whose Til Barsip lion inscriptions boast that he defeated 'Argishtu the Urartian' (usually dated c. 774 BC). Replacement: 'Shamshi-ilu the Turtan'.
(2) RAIDER 'Cimmerian Raiders' is anachronistic: Cimmerians are first attested c. 714 BC. Replacement: 'Etiuni Raiders'. Etiuni was the northern confederation Argishti campaigned against in 782 BC and that Erebuni was built to overawe.
(3) CAVALRY 'Median Cavalry' does not fit. Medes are attested from 835 BC, but in the Zagros far to the south-east, and they are never recorded fighting Urartu at Erebuni. Replacement: 'Assyrian Horsemen'. Assyrian cavalry existed as a fighting arm from Ashurnasirpal II (883 to 859 BC) onward.
(4) SPEARMAN 'Assyrian Spearmen' and SHIELD 'Assyrian Shieldbearers' are acceptable as contemporary enemies of Argishti I, with the caveat that no Assyrian army is recorded at Erebuni itself.
(5) RAM 'Siege Ram' is acceptable: Assyrian rams are well attested in 9th to 8th century reliefs.
(6) FLYER 'War Falcons' has no historical basis. It is a gameplay invention and is left as is because it makes no factual claim.

unitOverrides.name: Shamshi-ilu the Turtan
unitOverrides.why: Sargon II (r. 722 to 705 BC) came about 60 years after the founding. In Argishti I's day Assyria's real commander against Urartu was the turtan Shamshi-ilu, whose Til Barsip lions claim a victory over Argishti (c. 774 BC), under Shalmaneser IV (r. 783 to 773 BC).

unitOverrides.name: Etiuni Raiders
unitOverrides.why: Cimmerians are first attested c. 714 BC. The Etiuni confederation north of the Araxes was Erebuni's actual northern foe; Argishti campaigned against it in the year of the founding (782 BC).

unitOverrides.name: Assyrian Horsemen
unitOverrides.why: Medes lived far to the south-east in the Zagros and are never recorded fighting Urartu near Erebuni. Assyrian cavalry was an established arm of the armies that fought Argishti I.

notes:
Verification method and limits: the egress proxy blocked WebFetch and curl to every scholarly host tried (iranicaonline.org, wikipedia, britannica, livius, worldhistory.org, oracc, unesco, archive.org, cambridge, and others). Every claim was therefore checked against search-engine excerpts of these sources, not against full texts. The sources are: Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Erevan'; Britannica 'Erebuni' and 'Yerevan'; World History Encyclopedia 'Erebuni' (Wiener); Wikipedia 'Erebuni Fortress', 'Argishti I', 'Etiuni', 'Shamshi-ilu', 'Shalmaneser IV', 'Cimmerians', 'Founding of Rome', 'History of Yerevan'; S. Zaia, JNES 2018 (the Shamshi-ilu lion text naming Argishtu); Penn Museum 'Sargon's March'; Encyclopaedia Iranica / encyclopedia.com on the Medes; Armenian Weekly and AGBU on Yerevan 2800; Dezső on Assyrian cavalry. I could not reach Kroll et al., Biainili-Urartu or Zimansky's Ecology and Empire in full text.

Date consensus: 782 BC, the conventional date from the fifth regnal year. Variants are ca. 780 BC (Iranica) and 783 BC (Britannica's Yerevan entry).

Fixes made: (a) the 6,600 figure is now attributed to Argishti's Van annals and the men are identified as deported captives; (b) the 'oldest living city' and 'older than Rome' boasts are replaced with true statements (Yerevan takes Erebuni's name and dates its birth from the stone, decades before Rome's legendary 753 BC founding); (c) the anachronistic 'against Assyria and the steppe tribes' is replaced with Erebuni's real role, holding the Ararat plain and striking north toward Etiuni and Lake Sevan; (d) 'twenty-nine' is corrected to 'twenty-eight' centuries; (e) the em dashes are removed.

Name, tag and date are unchanged. The revised history is 479 characters, has no long dashes, and does not use 'honestly' or 'genuinely'. Urartu is presented as Urartu, not as 'Armenia'.

Owner-level issue: the era-0 roster's boss 'Sargon, King of Assyria' is wrong for this 782 BC battlefield. The overrides above are recommended.

target: Battlefield chronicle #1 "Vale of Tushpa" (era 0: Assyrian Invasion), LEVELS[1] in /root/.claude/uploads/169f7cc7-9178-569c-b36f-88a849db13cf/9e114454-index.html and e04fd670-index.scored-r5.html (lines 1280-1289)

claims.quote: In the 9th–8th centuries BC the kingdom of Urartu
claims.finding: Urartu became a unified kingdom in the mid-9th century BC. Sarduri I (c. 834-828 BC) built at Van and is generally taken as the founder of Tushpa. Tushpa stayed the royal centre through the 8th century and into the 7th (Rusa II's Rusahinili/Toprakkale was built next to it). UNESCO dates the capital to the 9th-6th centuries BC. So '9th-8th centuries' is true for the kingdom's height. The en dash has to go: write '9th and 8th'.
claims.sources: Livius, 'Tušpa (Van)' (livius.org/place/tuspa-van); UNESCO WHC Tentative List no. 6114 'Tushpa/Van Fortress, the Mound and the Old City of Van'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Tushpa'; Britannica, 'Urartu'

claims.quote: Biainili
claims.finding: 'Urartu' is the Assyrian name. From Ishpuini and Menua (late 9th c.) on, Urartian royal inscriptions call the kingdom Biainili, and Assyrian-Urartian bilinguals such as the Kelishin stele pair Urartian Biainili with Assyrian Nairi/Urartu.
claims.sources: Britannica, 'Urartu'; Kelishin bilingual as summarized in Urartu reference works (urartians.com.tr history page, encycloreader 'Urartu'); Zimansky, Ancient Ararat (cited)

claims.quote: the biblical land of Ararat
claims.finding: Hebrew 'Ararat' has the same consonants as Assyrian Urartu. The 'land of Ararat' where Sennacherib's sons fled (2 Kgs 19:37; Isa 37:38) and the 'kingdom of Ararat' of Jer 51:27 are the Urartian state. Gen 8:4 uses the same name for the mountains of the region.
claims.sources: Encyclopedia of the Bible, 'Ararat' (BibleGateway); Bible Hub Atlas, 'Ararat'; Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Ararat' (Jewish Virtual Library)

claims.quote: ruled these highlands from Tushpa, its capital carved into the Rock of Van
claims.finding: The citadel stands on the Rock of Van, a conglomerate/limestone ridge about 1.3 km long and up to about 100 m high on the eastern shore of Lake Van. Its walls sit on rock-cut terraces, and royal rock-cut tombs and cuneiform inscriptions are cut into the cliff. The capital itself was not carved into the rock: the lower town lay at its foot. Small fix: 'its citadel on the Rock of Van'.
claims.sources: UNESCO WHC Tentative List no. 6114; World History Encyclopedia, 'Tushpa'; Livius, 'Tušpa (Van)'

claims.quote: In 714 BC Sargon II of Assyria led his famous Eighth Campaign north
claims.finding: This is Sargon's 8th regnal-year campaign, 714 BC, known mainly from his 430-line 'Letter to the god Ashur' (Louvre AO 5372, first edited by Thureau-Dangin in 1912) and from the Khorsabad reliefs. The army went east through the Zagros into Mannea first and then turned north into Urartian provinces. The exact route has been argued over for a century. Most reconstructions (Thureau-Dangin, Zimansky 1990) put it around Lake Urmia, and a few take it near Lake Van.
claims.sources: Grant Frame, 'Sargon's March: A New Translation', Expedition 56.3 (Penn Museum); French Ministry of Culture, 'Orient cunéiforme: what it tells us' and 'Khorsabad: his military campaigns'; Zimansky, 'Urartian Geography and Sargon's Eighth Campaign', JNES 49 (1990); Harvard HIST 1039 project, 'The Eighth Campaign of Sargon II: A Historiographical Approach'

claims.quote: broke king Rusa I in the mountains
claims.finding: Rusa's defeat at Mount Uaush is in substance correct. Uaush is often identified with Mount Sahand, east of Lake Urmia, though that identification is debated. The battle is known only from Sargon's letter and annals: Sargon charged with his chariot and cavalry, and Rusa escaped on a mare. The annals also claim Rusa later stabbed himself, which some scholars doubt. The regnal number is contested. The traditional view makes Sargon's opponent Rusa son of Sarduri II ('Rusa I'). Roaf (2012, in Kroll et al., Biainili-Urartu), following Seidl, argues it was Rusa son of Erimena. The rewrite therefore drops the numeral.
claims.sources: Frame, Expedition 56.3; Oracc eCUT, 'Rusa, son of Sarduri II' (Urartian rulers and their inscriptions); Roaf 2012 in Kroll, Gruber, Hellwag, Roaf & Zimansky (eds.), Biainili-Urartu; academia.edu, 'Did Rusa commit suicide?'

claims.quote: sacked the holy city of Musasir
claims.finding: Musasir (Urartian Ardini) was the cult centre of the god Haldi, ruled by Urzana, and probably lay near the upper Great Zab between Lakes Urmia and Van. On the way home Sargon led a picked force against it. His texts say he plundered Urzana's palace and then the Haldi temple, and the booty is listed in detail. The Khorsabad reliefs show the gabled temple being stripped.
claims.sources: Britannica, 'Muṣaṣir'; Frame, Expedition 56.3; French Ministry of Culture, 'Orient cunéiforme'

claims.quote: But the fortress line held the heartland
claims.finding: No source says Urartian fortresses stopped Sargon. His letter claims he destroyed many fortified towns in Urartian provinces (Ulhu with Rusa's palace and canal, Sangibutu, Armarili, Ayadi and others), and that people fled to strongholds or the mountains. He then chose to strike Musasir on the way home, according to the Louvre/French ministry account after an omen. Tushpa was not attacked because it was not his target, not because a defensive line held. As written, the line implies an Urartian defensive victory in 714 that is not recorded.
claims.sources: Frame, Expedition 56.3; French Ministry of Culture, 'Khorsabad: his military campaigns'; Livius, 'Tušpa (Van)' ('Sargon marched almost unopposed through Urartu'); World History Encyclopedia, 'Tushpa' (Tushpa not directly attacked in 714)

claims.quote: Tushpa itself never fell to Assyria
claims.finding: The Eponym Chronicle entry for 735 BC reads 'to Urartu'. That year Tiglath-Pileser III shut Sarduri II up in Turushpa. In Luckenbill's translation of the annals he 'wrought great slaughter in front of the city gates' and set up his royal image facing the city, but he did not take it, and modern accounts call the siege unsuccessful. Sargon did not attack Tushpa in 714. Every excavated Urartian site, Tushpa included, was destroyed between c. 640 and 590 BC by unidentified attackers (Scythians and/or Medes are proposed), not by Assyria. Assyria itself fell in 612-609.
claims.sources: Assyrian Eponym Chronicle 735 BC (Records of the Past via sacred-texts.com; arar.sci.am 2025 article); Tiglath-Pileser III annals, Luckenbill ARAB I / RINAP 1 (quoted in World History Encyclopedia 'Tushpa'); Encyclopedia of the Bible, 'Tiglath-Pileser' ('In 735 he unsuccessfully besieged Tushpa'); EBSCO Research Starter, 'Tiglath-pileser III'; Metropolitan Museum essay, 'Urartu'

claims.quote: Hold the royal road, as the garrisons of Van once did.
claims.finding: Read after a 714 BC narrative, this suggests the Van garrisons fought off Sargon, which no source records. It is true of 735 BC, when Tushpa's citadel held against Tiglath-Pileser III. The line can stay word for word once the text names the 735 siege.
claims.sources: Tiglath-Pileser III annals via World History Encyclopedia 'Tushpa' and Livius 'Tušpa (Van)'; Frame, Expedition 56.3

claims.quote: 714 BC
claims.finding: As the date of a defence of the road to Tushpa against Sargon, 714 BC shows an event that did not happen. Sargon's army campaigned around Lake Urmia and in the Urartian provinces and then went to Musasir. Even the minority routes that bring him near Lake Van do not have him march on Tushpa. The one documented Assyrian assault on Tushpa is Tiglath-Pileser III's siege of 735 BC, which the defenders survived. Dating this battlefield 735 BC makes the defence real and heroic.
claims.sources: Assyrian Eponym Chronicle (735 'to Urartu'); Encyclopedia of the Bible 'Tiglath-Pileser'; Frame, Expedition 56.3; Zimansky JNES 49 (1990); Livius 'Tušpa (Van)'

claims.quote: The royal road to the citadel on Lake Van.
claims.finding: Tushpa's citadel stands on the eastern shore of Lake Van. 'Royal road' reads as a description (the road to the royal citadel), not the name of a known Urartian route, so it does not mislead.
claims.sources: Livius, 'Tušpa (Van)'; UNESCO WHC Tentative List no. 6114

revised.name: Vale of Tushpa
revised.tag: The royal road to the citadel on Lake Van.
revised.history: In the 9th and 8th centuries BC the kingdom of Urartu, Biainili to its kings and Ararat in the Bible, ruled these highlands from Tushpa, its citadel on the Rock of Van. In 735 BC Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria shut king Sarduri II in the city; his annals boast of slaughter at its gates, yet the citadel held. In 714 BC Sargon II routed Rusa and sacked Musasir, but never marched on Van: Tushpa itself never fell to Assyria. Hold the royal road, as the garrisons of Van once did.

rosterFit: A 714 BC battle on the road to Tushpa is not defensible as history. Sargon's 714 army never marched on Tushpa. The real Assyrian attack on the city came in 735 BC under Tiglath-Pileser III, so I recommend dating this battlefield 735 BC. For a 735 battle the era roster has these problems. (1) boss "Sargon, King of Assyria": wrong. Sargon reigned 722-705 BC; the king at Tushpa's gates in 735 was Tiglath-Pileser III. Replace with "Tiglath-Pileser III". (2) raider "Cimmerian Raiders": wrong. Cimmerians first appear in Assyrian intelligence letters of c. 714 BC, and they fought Urartu, never as Assyrian troops. Replace with "Itu'aean Archers": Aramean auxiliary archers recruited into the Assyrian army from Tiglath-Pileser III's reign onward. (3) cavalry "Median Cavalry": wrong. In this period the Medes were targets and tributaries of Assyrian campaigns (Tiglath-Pileser III in 744 and 737), not Assyrian horsemen. Replace with "Assyrian Horsemen"; Assyrian cavalry is well attested on Tiglath-Pileser III's Nimrud reliefs. (4) "Assyrian Spearmen", "Assyrian Shieldbearers" and "Siege Ram" fit: Tiglath-Pileser III's reliefs show shield-bearer and spearman pairs and wheeled battering rams. (5) flyer "War Falcons": no evidence for trained birds in Assyrian warfare. It is a game abstraction like the vishaps; leave it or rename it to something plainly mythic. If the owner keeps 714 BC and Sargon instead, the boss stays but the text must say he never marched on Tushpa (see notes). "Cimmerian Raiders" is then defensible as a separate enemy of Urartu that routed Rusa's army that year, though not Sargon's ally. "Median Cavalry" should still become "Assyrian Horsemen"; Sargon's letter has him charging at Uaush with his own cavalry.

unitOverrides.name: Tiglath-Pileser III
unitOverrides.why: The Assyrian king who besieged Tushpa in 735 BC (Eponym Chronicle 'to Urartu'; his annals). Sargon II only took the throne in 722 BC and never attacked Tushpa.

unitOverrides.name: Itu'aean Archers
unitOverrides.why: Cimmerians are not attested until c. 714 BC and fought against Urartu, never in the Assyrian army. Itu'aean Aramean auxiliary archers served Tiglath-Pileser III's army.

unitOverrides.name: Assyrian Horsemen
unitOverrides.why: The Medes were campaign targets and tributaries of Assyria in the 730s, not its cavalry. Native Assyrian cavalry is shown on Tiglath-Pileser III's Nimrud reliefs.

notes: Method limits: WebFetch and curl were blocked by the egress proxy for every scholarly host I tried (oracc/RINAP, Iranica, Wikipedia, Penn Museum PDF, JSTOR/Chicago, Cambridge, academia.edu, worldhistory.org, livius.org). Every check was therefore done through WebSearch result extracts. I could not read RINAP 1 (Tadmor & Yamada) or RINAP 2 (Frame) in full, so the Tiglath-Pileser quotation rests on the Luckenbill wording as cited by secondary sites. More than 10 sources were consulted: Frame (Penn Expedition 56.3); French Ministry of Culture Orient cunéiforme/Khorsabad pages; Zimansky JNES 1990 (via citations); the Harvard HIST 1039 route project; Livius 'Tušpa (Van)'; UNESCO Tentative List 6114; Britannica 'Muṣaṣir' and 'Urartu'; Oracc eCUT on Rusa and Roaf 2012 (via summary); Encyclopedia of the Bible 'Ararat' and 'Tiglath-Pileser'; EBSCO 'Tiglath-pileser III'; the Eponym Chronicle; the Met Museum 'Urartu' essay. Main errors in the original: (a) 'the fortress line held the heartland' invents an Urartian defensive success in 714; (b) the 714 date and the rally line together suggest Sargon was held off at Van; (c) the 'Rusa I' numeral is contested (Roaf 2012); (d) 'capital carved into the Rock' is loose. Rewrite: 479 characters, no long dashes, no banned words, tag unchanged (42 characters), name unchanged. The original rally line and 'Tushpa itself never fell to Assyria' are kept word for word. Date variant: some secondary sources put the Tushpa siege in 736, but the Eponym Chronicle gives 736 'to the foot of Mount Nal' and 735 'to Urartu', so the consensus is 735. Fallback if the owner wants to keep 714 BC and the Sargon boss (470 characters): "In the 9th and 8th centuries BC the kingdom of Urartu, the Biainili of its own kings and the biblical Ararat, ruled these highlands from Tushpa, its citadel on the Rock of Van. In 714 BC Sargon II of Assyria led his Eighth Campaign north; by his own account he routed king Rusa at Mount Uaush and sacked the holy city of Musasir. Yet he never marched on Tushpa, whose walls had defied Tiglath-Pileser III in 735 BC. Hold the royal road, as the garrisons of Van once did." With that fallback the battle is an openly hypothetical 'what if'. Related places in the file outside this target: the era story at line 1821 ('Sargon's armies march north ... toward the fortress of Tushpa') makes the same false suggestion and should be softened; the MAP_NODES comment at line 22895 says '714 BC' and needs updating if the date changes; the boss art (unitPaintBossSargon: a king in a chariot under a parasol) suits Tiglath-Pileser III equally, since his reliefs use the same iconography.

target: Battlefield chronicle #2 "Araxes Crossing" (era 1: Persian Invasion, 451 AD, Avarayr)

claims.quote: Araxes Crossing
claims.finding: The battle was not fought at a crossing of the Araxes. Iranica places Avarayr in the principality of Artaz, southeast of Maku, with the field 'along the banks of the Tlmut River (Rud-e Zangemar), apparently the Armeno-Persian frontier at that time'. The site is identified with modern Churs (38 deg 50' N, 45 deg 02' E, West Azerbaijan, Iran), which lies well south of the Araxes. The Tghmut is a tributary of the Araxes, but nothing in the sources describes the fighting as a river crossing. Suggested name: 'Avarayr Plain'.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Avarayr' (search extract: 'a village in Armenia in the principality of Artaz southeast of the Iranian town of Maku ... along the banks of the Tlmut River (Rud-e Zangemar)'); Wikipedia, 'Churs' (coordinates, identification with the Avarayr plain); Wikipedia, 'Avarayr Plain'

claims.quote: The plain of Avarayr — faith against the Immortals.
claims.finding: The plain of Avarayr is correct. 'The Immortals' is a modern gloss stated as fact (see the 'Immortal guard' claim below). The tag also uses an em dash, which the style rules ban. Replacement tag: 'On the Tghmut banks, faith against the shahanshah.' (50 characters).
claims.sources: Iranica 'Avarayr'; Michael B. Charles, 'The Sassanian Immortals', Iranica Antiqua 46 (2011) 289-313

claims.quote: 451 AD
claims.finding: The year 451 is certain. The day varies by source: Armenian tradition and most popular accounts give 26 May 451, while Iranica's Yazdegerd II article and some scholarship give 2 June 451. Both dates fall on a Saturday in the Julian calendar, and Julian Pentecost that year was 27 May. Keeping the year only is the safe choice.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Yazdegerd II' (search extract: Mushkan Niusalavurt 'defeated the Mamikonian's forces on 2 June 451'); Wikipedia 'Battle of Avarayr' (26 May 451); my own computation of the Julian calendar (Easter 451 = 8 April)

claims.quote: In 451 AD Yazdegerd II, shahanshah of Sasanian Persia, commanded Armenia to renounce Christianity for Zoroastrianism.
claims.finding: Yazdegerd II (r. 438/9-457) did order the Armenians to convert to Zoroastrianism. The order came through Mihr-Narseh's edict, which Catholicos Hovsep and 17 bishops answered with a refusal. But Iranica dates the decree to 449, not 451. 451 is the year of the battle, so the original puts the decree two years late. Fix: keep the sentence word for word but drop 'In 451 AD', and move 451 to the battle sentence.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Avarayr' ('decree issued in 449 by the Sasanian king, Yazdegerd II, ordering the Armenians to convert'); Iranica, 'Łazar Pʿarpecʿi' (Mihr-Narseh's edict, reply of Catholicos Yovsep and 17 bishops); Iranica 'Yazdegerd II' (persecutions 449-51)

claims.quote: Sparapet Vardan Mamikonian answered him on the plain of Avarayr
claims.finding: Vardan Mamikonian (c. 387-451), head of the Mamikonian house, held the hereditary Mamikonian office of sparapet (commander-in-chief) and led the Armenian army at Avarayr. Yazdegerd II was not on the field himself. The Persian army was led by Mushkan Niusalavurt, whom Mihr-Narseh had appointed. The rewrite therefore says Vardan 'met the Persians' instead of 'answered him'.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Mamikonean' (sparapet office hereditary in the clan); Iranica 'Yazdegerd II' (Mushkan Niusalavurt dispatched); Wikipedia 'Mushkan Niusalavurt'

claims.quote: with some 66,000 Armenians
claims.finding: 66,000 is Yeghishe's figure ('a mighty force of sixty-six thousand men, including cavalry and infantry'). Modern summaries call it possibly exaggerated, and some popular accounts give 60,000 instead. Under the owner's rules it has to be credited to him: 'Yeghishe counts 66,000 Armenians'.
claims.sources: Yeghishe (Elishe), History of Vardan and the Armenian War, as quoted on the Armenian Church (Eastern Diocese) page 'The Eve of Avarayr: St. Vartan's Address to His Troops'; Wikipedia 'Battle of Avarayr' ('perhaps exaggerated')

claims.quote: against a far larger army
claims.finding: Every source presents the Persians as more numerous. But the numbers in circulation (300,000; 200,000; 'three times larger') are unsourced or inflated chronicle-tradition figures, with no reliable count behind them. 'Far larger' as plain fact goes beyond the evidence. The rewrite keeps a modest 'a larger host' inside the clause credited to Yeghishe.
claims.sources: World History Encyclopedia, 'Byzantine-Armenian Relations' (Persian army 'said to be three times larger'); Wikipedia 'Battle of Avarayr' infobox (300,000); Providence magazine 'Avarayr: A Short History' (60,000 vs 200,000)

claims.quote: with war elephants
claims.finding: Both 5th-century historians describe Persian elephants at Avarayr. Yeghishe says the Persian commander drew up elephants, with a commander mounted on one 'as if in a fortified city'. Ghazar Parpetsi says the Armenians held their own until the elephant corps was brought up, and describes men trampled by elephants.
claims.sources: Ghazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians, trans. R. Bedrosian (attalus.org gp5, via search extract); Yeghishe (extract of the battle narrative via search); Iranica 'Avarayr'

claims.quote: and the Immortal guard
claims.finding: Yeghishe does report an elite Persian unit at Avarayr, but he calls it the 'matean gund' (also 'matenik gund'). Chaumont (1973) linked this term to Persian 'gund-i madiyan', which Henning glossed as 'the principal battalion'. Armenian scholarship identifies it with the elite cavalry that Greek writers (Procopius, Malalas, Theophanes) call 'Athanatoi', the Immortals. 'Immortals' is therefore a Greco-Roman label, and Michael Charles argues that Sasanian 'Immortals' in Western sources 'may owe more to classicizing fancy than to historical reality'. The unit was cavalry, not a guard of spearmen. Stating 'the Immortal guard' as fact overstates the evidence, so the rewrite drops it.
claims.sources: Michael B. Charles, 'The Sassanian Immortals', Iranica Antiqua 46 (2011) 289-313 (abstract via Southern Cross University research portal); Wikipedia 'Immortals (Sasanian Empire)' citing Chaumont 1973, Henning 1942, Nyberg 1974; Armenian Wikipedia 'Matyan gund' (Yeghishe reports it deployed against Vardan at Avarayr)

claims.quote: Vardan fell and the field was lost
claims.finding: Vardan was killed and the Persians held the field. Yeghishe's casualty figures are 1,036 Armenian dead and 3,544 Persian dead. Iranica calls the Persian victory Pyrrhic: 'the king, faced with troubles elsewhere, was forced to allow the Armenians to worship as they chose'. Vasak Siuni and the noble houses that followed him had gone over to Persia beforehand. The original does not mention this, which is an omission rather than an error.
claims.sources: Iranica 'Avarayr'; Wikipedia 'Battle of Avarayr' (casualties after Yeghishe); Wikipedia 'Vasak Siwni'

claims.quote: yet the mountain war that followed forced the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484, winning Armenia her faith
claims.finding: This squeezes 33 years into one sentence. After 451, holdouts continued in the fortresses, nobles and clergy were deported, and Yazdegerd eased the pressure. Persecution came back under Peroz, and in 481/482 Vardan's nephew Vahan Mamikonian (son of Vardan's brother Hmayeak) began a new revolt. The Treaty of Nvarsak was concluded in 484 between Vahan and the envoys of Balash, after Peroz was killed fighting the Hephthalites. It guaranteed freedom of worship, and Vahan became marzpan in 485. The 451 war did not by itself force Nvarsak. Rewritten as 'after a new revolt his nephew Vahan won freedom of worship by the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484'.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Treaty of Nvarsak'; Wikipedia 'Vahan I Mamikonian'; Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Mamikonean' and 'Łazar Pʿarpecʿi' (Ghazar is the source for Vahan's war); Iranica 'Avarayr' ('persecuted Christianity in Armenia again within two generations')

claims.quote: The Church numbers the fallen among the saints.
claims.finding: The Armenian Apostolic Church honours St. Vardan and his 1,036 companions as the Holy Vardanants martyrs, with a feast on the Thursday before Great Lent. Kept word for word.
claims.sources: Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin, 'Feast of the Holy Vardanants' (armenianchurch.org, 12 Feb 2026); Western Prelacy, 'Divine Liturgy on the Feast of Sts. Vartanants'; Wikipedia 'Vardan Mamikonian'

revised.name: Avarayr Plain
revised.tag: On the Tghmut banks, faith against the shahanshah.
revised.history: Yazdegerd II, shahanshah of Sasanian Persia, commanded Armenia to renounce Christianity for Zoroastrianism. In 451 sparapet Vardan Mamikonian met the Persians on the plain of Avarayr; Yeghishe counts 66,000 Armenians against a larger host with war elephants. Vardan fell and the field was lost, yet the faith held: after a new revolt his nephew Vahan won freedom of worship by the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484. The Church numbers the fallen among the saints. Stand where Vardan stood.

rosterFit: Boss 'Yazdegerd II' is wrong for this battlefield. The shahanshah was not at Avarayr; the Persian army was led by Mushkan Niusalavurt (Yeghishe; Iranica 'Yazdegerd II'). Replace with 'Mushkan Niusalavurt'. Spearman 'Immortal Spearmen' is doubly off. 'Immortals' is a Greco-Roman label whose Sasanian reality is disputed (Charles 2011). Yeghishe's unit, the matean gund, was elite cavalry, not spear infantry. Sasanian foot soldiers were the paygan, light infantry with spears and wicker shields, so replace with 'Paygan Spearmen'. Shield 'Savaran Shieldbearers' mislabels the unit: savaran means the cavalry, so it cannot name a foot unit of shieldbearers. Replace with 'Paygan Shieldbearers'. Ram 'War Elephant' is correct: Yeghishe and Ghazar both describe Persian elephants at Avarayr. Cavalry 'Cataphracts' is acceptable; Sasanian heavy horse was the core of Mushkan's army. 'Savaran Cataphracts' would move the Savaran name to the role it belongs to, but this is optional. Raider 'Persian Skirmishers' is generic and acceptable. Flyer 'Simurgh Fledglings' is mythological (the Simurgh of Iranian legend), a fantasy unit rather than a historical claim. Leave it as is.

unitOverrides.name: Mushkan Niusalavurt
unitOverrides.why: Yazdegerd II was not at Avarayr. Mushkan Niusalavurt commanded the Persian army in the battle (Yeghishe; Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Yazdegerd II').

unitOverrides.name: Paygan Spearmen
unitOverrides.why: The 'Immortals' label for Sasanians is a classicizing Greco-Roman term (Charles, Iranica Antiqua 2011). Yeghishe's elite matean gund was cavalry, not spear infantry. Paygan were the Sasanian foot soldiers armed with short spears.

unitOverrides.name: Paygan Shieldbearers
unitOverrides.why: Savaran means the cavalry, so it cannot name a foot unit of shieldbearers. Sasanian infantry (paygan) carried wicker or light wooden shields.

target: Battlefield chronicle #3 "Dvin Gates" (era 2: Arab Invasion, 7th century AD)

claims.quote: Dvin was the great capital of early-medieval Armenia
claims.finding: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Khosrov III Kotak (4th c.) built Dvin as a new capital north of Artaxata. After the Arsacid monarchy ended in 428 it was the capital of Persian Armenia and the marzpan's seat. After 640 it was the caliph's governor's seat until 173/789.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Dvin' (iranicaonline.org/articles/dvin); Wikipedia 'Dvin (ancient city)' (search excerpts)

claims.quote: seat of the catholicos
claims.finding: Iranica says the catholicos probably sat at Dvin from the second half of the 5th century. Other summaries date the catholicosate's residence there from c. 465/485 to the late 9th or early 10th century (931). The Councils of Dvin (506, 554) met there. It was the patriarchal seat in 640.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Dvin'; Wikipedia 'Seats of the Catholicos of Armenians', 'Second Council of Dvin' (search excerpts)

claims.quote: a city of merchants
claims.finding: Procopius, Wars II.25, says many merchants traded at Doubios (Dvin), bringing goods from India, Iberia, nearly every nation of Persia and some Roman lands.
claims.sources: Procopius, History of the Wars II.25 (LacusCurtius/Thayer text, search excerpt)

claims.quote: the cathedral of St. Gregory
claims.finding: Excavations at Dvin uncovered the cathedral of St. Gregory the Illuminator. It began as a 3rd-century three-nave building, became a church in the 4th century, was rebuilt with fortifications after destruction in the early 7th century, and was rebuilt again as a cross-winged domed church in the mid-7th century (Kafadaryan 1952).
claims.sources: armeniapedia 'Dvin Ruins'; barnard.nl 'In the shadow of Mount Ararat' (citing Kafadaryan 1952)

claims.quote: In 640 AD
claims.finding: Sebeos (Thomson tr.) dates the capture to a Friday, 20 Tre. I converted this from the Armenian calendar (1 Navasard 552 = 11 July): it gives 6 October 640 (Julian), which was a Friday. Bedrosian's '30 Tre' would fall on a Monday, so it does not fit. Iranica gives 17 Shawwal 19 / 6 October 640, and Garsoian (Hovannisian ed.) gives 6 October 640. The variant is 642: Ghevond puts it in the 2nd year of Constans II, and some modern summaries give 6 January 642. The consensus is 6 October 640.
claims.sources: Sebeos ch. 42 (Thomson/Howard-Johnston 1999; Bedrosian tr.); Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Dvin'; N. Garsoian, 'The Arab Invasions and the Rise of the Bagratuni (640-884)' in Hovannisian ed., The Armenian People vol. 1; Ghevond ch. 1 (Bedrosian tr.); my own Julian weekday calculation

claims.quote: the first Arab army
claims.finding: Sebeos presents this as the first Ishmaelite entry into Armenia. Arab sources record a first expedition under Iyad ibn Ghanm in 639/640 that reached Bitlis, probably part of the same push from the Jazira. The 640 strike was a raid, not a conquest. The Muslim sources place the conquest proper in 645/6 and after, under Habib ibn Maslama. Neither Sebeos nor Ghevond, as excerpted, names the commander of the Dvin raid.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Arminiya' and 'Arab invasion of Armenia' (citing Canard/Ter-Ghewondyan and Arabic sources); Garsoian in Hovannisian ed.; Sebeos ch. 42

claims.quote: burst over the Araxes
claims.finding: The recorded route runs from Taron and Bznunik through Aliovit and the Berkri valley, then Kogovit, into Ayrarat. Garsoian: 'reached through Aghiovit and Kogovit to the undefended capital of Duin'. Sebeos names the Metsamor bridge as the crossing point: Armenian troops crossed it and broke it, and the raiders still got over, guided by Vardik, prince of Mokk. Coming from Kogovit, the raiders would have had to cross the Araxes somewhere, but no source I found describes that crossing. The attested detail is the Metsamor.
claims.sources: Sebeos ch. 42 (Bedrosian tr., arak29.org PDF excerpt); Garsoian in Hovannisian ed., The Armenian People vol. 1

claims.quote: and stormed it
claims.finding: Sebeos: on the fifth day, a Friday, they lit fires and drove the guards off the wall with smoke and arrows. They then set up ladders, scaled the wall and opened the gates from inside. Ghevond adds that the fighting men were away with prince Theodoros Rshtuni.
claims.sources: Sebeos ch. 42 (Bedrosian tr.); Ghevond ch. 1 (Bedrosian tr.)

claims.quote: the chroniclers wrote of thirty-five thousand carried away
claims.finding: Sebeos records 35,000 captives from Dvin; his chapter heading reads 'captivity of 35,000 men from Dvin'. Ghevond says 'the women and children, some 35,000 souls'. The figure belongs to the chroniclers and is correctly attributed. Some modern summaries add '12,000 slain', but I did not trace that to a primary source, and the text leaves it out, correctly.
claims.sources: Sebeos ch. 42 (12historians.armeniancathedral.org index; Bedrosian tr.); Ghevond ch. 1 (Bedrosian tr., almuslih.org PDF excerpt)

claims.quote: The city rose again and was fought over for two centuries more.
claims.finding: Dvin was contested for nearly six centuries after 640, not two. Events: Habib ibn Maslama's capitulation treaty with Dabil under Uthman (c. 645-654), described by al-Baladhuri; Arab ostikan seat to 789; Sajid control and the failed Byzantine siege of 927; the 893 earthquake; Shaddadid rule and Abu'l-Aswar's defence against three Byzantine attacks in the 1040s; Seljuk occupation in 1064; Georgian capture in 1173 and again in 1201-1203; total destruction by the Mongols in 1236.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Dvin (ancient city)', 'Siege of Dvin (927)', '893 Dvin earthquake' (search excerpts); al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, treaty of Habib ibn Maslama (via MDPI Religions 12/2/138); Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Dvin'

claims.quote: Dvin's walls have been rebuilt before, and will be again.
claims.finding: This rally line is true. Heraclius sacked Dvin in 624 and it recovered; the cathedral was rebuilt with fortifications in the early 7th century; the city rose again after 640. The original's em dash must be replaced.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Sack of Dvin (624)'; barnard.nl/armeniapedia (Kafadaryan 1952)

claims.quote: Twin roads besiege the cathedral capital.
claims.finding: A gameplay framing for the two-path map, not a historical claim. 'Cathedral capital' fits Dvin, seat of the catholicos and the cathedral of St. Gregory. No change needed.
claims.sources: As above (Iranica 'Dvin'; Dvin excavation summaries)

revised.name: Dvin Gates
revised.tag: Twin roads besiege the cathedral capital.
revised.history: Dvin was the great capital of early-medieval Armenia: seat of the catholicos, a city of merchants and the cathedral of St. Gregory. In 640 AD the first Arab army came down through Kogovit, crossed the Metsamor and stormed it with smoke, arrows and ladders; the chroniclers wrote of thirty-five thousand carried away. The city rose again and was fought over for six centuries more. Hold both roads to the gates: Dvin's walls have been rebuilt before, and will be again.

rosterFit:
Mostly fits, with two fixes.
(1) ram "Battering Ram" is wrong for this battle. Sebeos says the Arabs took Dvin by driving the guards off the wall with smoke and arrows, then setting up ladders, climbing in and opening the gates. No ram is recorded. Replace with "Scaling Ladders" (high confidence).
(2) cavalry "Camel Riders" is a weak fit. In 640 the Arabs used camels mainly for marching and baggage, and fought on horseback or on foot. This raid crossed the mountain passes of Taron, Aliovit and Kogovit into Ayrarat. Replace with "Arab Horsemen" (moderate confidence).
boss "The Caliph's General" is acceptable and deliberately generic. Umar was caliph. Neither Sebeos nor Ghevond, as excerpted, names the raid's commander. Arab sources credit Iyad ibn Ghanm with the first 639/640 expedition, which reached Bitlis, but tying him to Dvin is uncertain. worldhistory.org's 'Khalid' is unreliable: Khalid ibn al-Walid had been dismissed by 638. Do not name anyone.
raider "Desert Skirmishers", spearman "Caliphate Spearmen" and shield "Mailed Swordsmen" are fine for a Rashidun-era army. The skirmishers also fit Sebeos's arrow fire on the walls.
flyer "Desert Hawks" is a fantasy unit with no historical claim; harmless.

unitOverrides.name: Scaling Ladders
unitOverrides.why: Sebeos says Dvin fell to smoke, arrows and ladders scaled over the wall, with the gates then opened from inside. No battering ram is recorded.

unitOverrides.name: Arab Horsemen
unitOverrides.why: In the Rashidun era, camels carried troops on the march but horsemen did the fighting. The 640 raid crossed mountain passes from Taron through Kogovit into Ayrarat. Moderate confidence.

Method caveat: WebFetch was blocked by the egress proxy for every host I tried (Wikipedia, iranicaonline, attalus, arak29, archive.org, tertullian, cristoraul). All evidence comes from WebSearch result excerpts of these sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Dvin'; Garsoian's chapter in Hovannisian ed.; Sebeos (Bedrosian tr., with Thomson/Howard-Johnston for the date); Ghevond (Bedrosian tr.); Procopius Wars II.25; al-Baladhuri via MDPI; Wikipedia articles on Dvin, Arminiya, Arab invasion of Armenia, the 927 siege and the 893 earthquake; armeniapedia and barnard.nl on the cathedral.

Date: I checked Sebeos's '20 Tre, Friday' myself. It converts to 6 October 640 Julian, which is a Friday. Bedrosian's reading '30 Tre' would be Monday 16 October, which supports Thomson's reading and the 640 consensus. The 642 variant (Ghevond: 2nd year of Constans II; '6 January 642' in some summaries) is the minority date.

Changes, three in total:

If the owner prefers to keep the Araxes, an Araxes crossing is geographically implied but not described in any source.

claims.quote: Arab armies first broke into Armenia in 640 AD
claims.finding: Arabic sources put the first raid into Armenia in 639/640, led by Iyad ibn Ghanim, who got as far as Bitlis. Sebeos and Catholicos John date the first Arab capture of Dvin to 640. The Muslim sources date the formal conquest later, to 645/646 under Habib ibn Maslama.
claims.sources: Sebeos, History (via Wikipedia 'Arminiya' and 'Dvin (ancient city)', which cite Sebeos and John Catholicos); Hovannisian ed., The Armenian People vol. I (Ter-Ghewondyan/Garsoian chapters, as summarised in search results)

claims.quote: sacked Dvin
claims.finding: Dvin was stormed during the first Arab invasion. Most sources follow Sebeos and give 640. One variant dates the storming to 6 January 642. The captive figure (35,000) is kept on the separate Dvin Gates card, where it is already attributed to the chroniclers.
claims.sources: Sebeos via Wikipedia 'Dvin (ancient city)'; Wikipedia 'Arminiya'

claims.quote: and ruled through emirs for two centuries
claims.finding: Until about 700 Armenia paid tribute but kept its own princes. Direct rule came with Muhammad ibn Marwan's campaigns (c. 700 to 705). After that the caliphs ruled through governors (Armenian 'ostikan', seated at Dvin) until 884. Arab emirates (the Qaysites and others; see Ter-Ghewondyan) settled inside Armenia in the 8th and 9th centuries. Saying they ruled 'through emirs' alone leaves out the governors. 'Two centuries' is a fair round figure for 640s to 884. The rewrite says 'the caliphs ruled through governors and emirs'.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Arminiya' and 'Ostikan'; Ter-Ghewondyan, The Arab Emirates in Bagratid Armenia (by title and scope); Ghevond's History (indexed at historians.armeniancathedral.org)

claims.quote: In 885 the Bagratuni kings restored the Armenian crown
claims.finding: One man restored the crown: Ashot I Bagratuni. 'Kings' in the plural is wrong. Caliph al-Mu'tamid sent him a crown in 884, and Armenian tradition dates the coronation to 885, so modern works give 884 or 885. Byzantine Emperor Basil I also sent a crown, c. 886. 885 is acceptable; the rewrite names Ashot Bagratuni.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Ashot I of Armenia' and 'Bagratid Armenia'; Vardan Areveltsi and Kirakos Gandzaketsi (as cited there); Britannica 'Bagratid dynasty'

claims.quote: when the Sajid emir Yusuf invaded in 909
claims.finding: In 908 Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, Sajid emir of Azerbaijan, gave a crown to Gagik Artsruni of Vaspurakan. In 909 the two of them invaded Smbat I's kingdom: Yusuf took Nakhchivan, then Siunik, and wintered in Dvin. In 910 he beat Smbat's sons Ashot and Mushegh at Dzknavachar in Nig, north of Yerevan, and Mushegh was captured and poisoned. In 913 Smbat was besieged in Kapuyt Berd (Erenjak, Nakhchivan) and gave himself up. He was killed in 914 (some scholars say 913). Sources disagree on the place: Yusuf's article has him executed before the walls of Erenjak, Smbat's has him put to death at Dvin; both say his body was crucified at Dvin.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj', 'Smbat I of Armenia', 'Gagik I Artsruni'; Hovhannes Draskhanakerttsi via hy.wikipedia 'Battle of Dzknavachar'; Stepanos Asoghik III.4 (title located at historians.armeniancathedral.org); Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Sajids' (search summary)

claims.quote: the war came north into the wooded gorges of Lori and Tashir
claims.finding: No source I found places the fighting of 909-910 in Tashir. The known war ran through Nakhchivan, Siunik, Dvin, Nig/Dzknavachar and Erenjak, which is the centre and south. The north did become a theatre in 914, in two ways: Yusuf campaigned in Georgia (Tbilisi, Kakheti, Kartli, and the siege of Q'ueli where Gobron was martyred), and after Smbat's death his son Ashot II and brother Abas, helped by Georgian rulers, drove Yusuf's garrisons out of Bagrevand, Shirak and Gugark as far as Tiflis. Tashir is a canton of Gugark. The rewrite moves the card to 914 and states only the Gugark claim.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Sajid invasion of Georgia', 'Siege of Queli', 'Ashot II of Armenia'; hayazg.info 'Ashot II' (Armenian Encyclopedia, which cites Draskhanakerttsi); ru.wikipedia 'Ashot II Zhelezny'

claims.quote: Lori
claims.finding: Lori Berd was built by King David I Anhoghin of the Kiurikid kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget (reigned c. 989-1048). The kingdom itself was founded in 979, with its capital at Matsnaberd; the capital moved to Lori only in 1065, after Samshvilde was lost. The region's name comes from that fortress. In 910-914 the area was called Tashir, a canton of Gugark recorded since Movses Khorenatsi.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Lori Fortress', 'Kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget', 'Lori (historic province)', 'Tashir'; armeniapedia 'Lori Berd'

claims.quote: where fortress and canyon carried the resistance
claims.finding: Smbat I made his last stand at Kapuyt Berd in Erenjak (Nakhchivan), not in the northern gorges. After 914 the northern resistance was real: Ashot II was crowned by Adarnase IV of Iberia (914 by most modern dating, or after 915/916) and cleared garrisons from Gugark. No source credits 'fortress and canyon' in Tashir.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Smbat I of Armenia', 'Ashot II of Armenia', 'Adarnase IV of Iberia'; hayazg.info 'Ashot II'

claims.quote: Out of that survival grew a golden age
claims.finding: Calling it a golden age is interpretation, but common: after Ashot II, Armenia flourished under Abas, Ashot III (Ani made capital in 961) and Smbat II. I dropped the phrase only to stay within the character budget.
claims.sources: UNESCO WHC 777 ('revival of Armenian architecture in the 10th and 11th centuries'); Wikipedia 'Bagratid Armenia'

revised.name: Tashir Gates

claims.quote: In 921 AD
claims.finding: 921 is the traditional date. Armenian Wikipedia, the Soviet Armenian Encyclopedia tradition, English Wikipedia and Dymydyuk (2018) all use it. Other sources disagree. English Wikipedia's Kakavaberd article, citing Draskhanakerttsi, puts Beshir's attack on Kakavaberd (Geghi), which followed the Sevan defeat, in 924. An Armenian encyclopedic entry gives 'summer of 925'. Ter-Ghewondyan, as cited by Takirtakoglou (Banber Matenadarani 32, 2021), says Nasr went back to Azerbaijan in 924 and left Bashir behind as his deputy. Encyclopaedia Iranica says Yusuf was captured in July 919 and released in May 922. If Beshir served Yusuf, a later date is therefore quite plausible. The text keeps 921 as the most widely used date and names 924 as the variant.

Garsoian 1976), as cited by Takirtakoglou, 'Ashot II Yerkat and the Byzantines', Banber Matenadarani 32 (2021); Dymydyuk, 'Arms and Armour of Bagratid Armenian Noblemen'

claims.quote: the Arab general Beshir
claims.finding: Beshir (Bashir) served Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, the Sajid emir of Azerbaijan, who also governed Armenia for the caliph. Ter-Ghewondyan's chronology makes him deputy to the Sajid governor Nasr. The Sajids were an Iranian Muslim dynasty of Sogdian origin from Ushrusana. None of the sources found give Beshir's own ethnicity, so calling him 'Arab' follows Armenian tradition and is not an established fact. Rewritten as 'general of the Sajid emir Yusuf'.
claims.sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica 'BANŪ SĀJ'; Wikipedia 'Sajid dynasty' (excerpt); Ter-Ghewondyan via Takirtakoglou 2021; Armenian sources (Beshr, 'a general of Emir Yusuf')

claims.quote: marching on the shores of Lake Sevan
claims.finding: All accounts put Beshir's army on the shore of Lake Sevan facing the king, who was on Sevan island.
claims.sources: hy.wikipedia 'Սևանի ճակատամարտ'; Wikipedia 'Battle of Sevan'; Dymydyuk citing Draskhanakerttsi

claims.quote: king Ashot II — called Erkat, 'the Iron'
claims.finding: Ashot II (r. 914 to 929) is usually known as Erkat/Yerkat, 'the Iron'. The long dash is removed in the rewrite.
claims.sources: Garsoian in Hovannisian ed., The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times vol. 1 (search excerpt: 'usually known as Erkat ("the Iron King")'); Wikipedia 'Ashot II of Armenia'

claims.quote: gathered only a few dozen loyal men
claims.finding: Draskhanakerttsi, a contemporary and the reigning Catholicos, writes that the king 'immediately launched eleven ships with seventy azats and servants aboard', all men with 'well-bent bows' who were expert archers. This is the Maksoudian translation as quoted by Dymydyuk. Armenian accounts say Ashot had shut himself up on the island 'with a small military detachment'. Some popular retellings say ten boats with seven archers each, but the direct quotation says eleven. 'A few dozen' is roughly right for the sortie, but the figure comes from the chronicle and should be credited to it. The rewrite does that.
claims.sources: Hovhannes Draskhanakerttsi, History of Armenia, tr. Maksoudian (1987), as quoted in Dymydyuk; hy.wikipedia 'Սևանի ճակատամարտ'

claims.quote: Fighting with the great lake at his back
claims.finding: Ashot was not fighting with the lake behind him. He sailed out from the island and attacked from the water, and his archers shot into Beshir's men massed on the shore.
claims.sources: Draskhanakerttsi via Dymydyuk; Wikipedia 'Battle of Sevan' (excerpts)

claims.quote: he broke the invaders
claims.finding: Draskhanakerttsi, as quoted, says the enemy could not stand the stream of arrows and fled. After the Sevan defeat, Beshir attacked the fortress of Geghi (Kakavaberd) and was beaten again, by Gevorg Marzpetuni. The rewrite credits this to the chronicler.
claims.sources: Draskhanakerttsi via Dymydyuk and Wikipedia; Wikipedia 'Kakavaberd'; Armenian sources on Beshr's defeat at Geghi

claims.quote: and turned the war
claims.finding: Armenian popular and Soviet-era histories do call Sevan a turning point, after which Ashot cleared central and northern Armenia. But the war did not end there. The Sajid governor Nasr still held Dvin, and a Byzantine army failed to take Dvin from him in 927. The chronicle should not claim a decisive strategic reversal as fact.
claims.sources: Wikipedia 'Battle of Sevan' (turning-point claim); Wikipedia 'Siege of Dvin (927)' (search excerpt); Ter-Ghewondyan via Takirtakoglou 2021

claims.quote: within years the emirs' grip on Armenia was finished
claims.finding: False. Muslim emirs kept Dvin and other Armenian cities long after Ashot II died in 929. The Sajid line ended around 929, but Dvin then went to other Muslim dynasties (Sallarids, then Shaddadids), and emirates such as the Kaysites of Manazkert lasted into the 11th century. Ter-Ghewondyan's book on the Arab emirates of Bagratid Armenia is about exactly this survival. Removed.
claims.sources: Ter-Ghewondyan, The Arab Emirates in Bagratid Armenia; Encyclopaedia Iranica 'SHADDADIDS' and 'BANŪ SĀJ'

claims.quote: The chroniclers say the lake itself seemed to fight beside him.
claims.finding: I found no such statement in Draskhanakerttsi or in any secondary account I consulted. It looks invented and is attributed to the chroniclers without support. Removed.
claims.sources: Draskhanakerttsi excerpts via Dymydyuk and Wikipedia; hy.wikipedia; Kakavaberd and Battle of Sevan articles

claims.finding: A rally line with no factual claim beyond Ashot's stand at Sevan, which is attested. Kept verbatim.

claims.finding: A poetic tag consistent with the attested setting (Ashot on Sevan island). It makes no false factual claim, so it is kept unchanged at 50 characters.

revised.history: In 921 AD (some scholars date it to 924), Beshir, general of the Sajid emir Yusuf, marched on the shores of Lake Sevan. King Ashot II, called Erkat, 'the Iron', held the island with a small band. Hovhannes Draskhanakerttsi, who lived through these years, writes that the king sailed out in eleven boats with seventy bowmen and their arrows drove Beshir's host from the shore; Gevorg Marzpetuni beat him again at Geghi. Make your stand where the Iron King made his.

Replace with 'Beshir, Sajid General'. (2) cavalry 'Camel Riders' (with the camel sprite) is wrong for an army from Azerbaijan fighting in the Armenian highlands, and no source mentions camels at Sevan. Replace with 'Sajid Horsemen'. target: Battlefield chronicle #6 "Gyumri Road" (era 3: Ottoman Invasion, 16th century AD)

claims.quote: By the 16th century the highlands had become the battlefield of two empires.
claims.finding: Ottoman-Safavid wars ran 1532-1555, 1578-1590 and 1603-1618. The Peace of Amasya (29 May 1555) split Armenia: the west went to the Ottomans and the east to the Safavids. According to Wikipedia, Yerevan changed hands fourteen times between 1514 and 1736.
claims.sources: English Wikipedia (June 2023 dump): 'Peace of Amasya', 'Iranian Armenia (1502-1828)', 'Ottoman-Safavid War (1578-1590)'; Lynch, Armenia: Travels and Studies I (1901), Erivan chapter ('continually disputed between the Sultans and... the Persian Shahs')

claims.quote: Ottoman and Safavid armies crossed the plain of Shirak again and again
claims.finding: Shirak sat on the frontier. Armenian Wikipedia's article on Shirak province says that in the 15th and 16th centuries Shirak was repeatedly devastated by Turkmen, Safavid and Ottoman invasions. It also says that after 1555 the Akhurian (Arpa Chai) split Shirak, with the east bank going to Persia and the west bank to the Ottomans. Recorded crossings: in August 1583 Ferhad Pasha's army marched from Kars to Erivan through Shuragel (Shirak). In 1604 Shah Abbas advanced on Kars. Lynch (citing Ritter) equates Shuragel with Armenian Shirak.
claims.sources: Armenian Wikipedia 'Shirak (gavar)' and 'Gyumri'; Turkish Wikipedia 'Revan'in Zapti'; Lynch I (1901) note 61; English Wikipedia 'Iranian Armenia (1502-1828)'

claims.quote: janissaries and great bombards against stone villages
claims.finding: Janissaries were there: Lala Mustafa set out with the kapikulu household troops on 28 April 1578, and by the 16th century janissaries were musketeers. Ottoman guns are recorded at fortresses, not against Shirak villages. For example, Ferhad Pasha mounted 50 sahi guns in the new Erivan fortress in 1583. 'Great bombards' suggests 15th-century giant siege guns, and I found no evidence for their use against villages here. Dropped from the rewrite.
claims.sources: Turkish Wikipedia 'Cildir Muharebesi', 'Revan'in Zapti'; English Wikipedia 'Janissary'

claims.quote: in the 1570s the Ottomans took the country around Kumayri
claims.finding: Kumayri (Gumri) was in the Safavid province of Erivan (Chukhur-e Sa'd) and stayed Safavid through the 1570s. Under the Peace of Amasya, Kars had been declared neutral and its fortress razed. In 1579 Lala Mustafa Pasha came to Kars on Murad III's order and rebuilt it (that year the Holy Apostles church became a mosque and the Grand Mosque was restored). Kars lies about 70 km west of Gyumri, beyond the Arpa Chai. Eastern Shirak fell in 1583: Ferhad Pasha left Kars on 11 August 1583, fortified Shuregel (Shirak) and Talin as sanjaks, and entered Erivan without a fight in mid-September after Tokmak Khan withdrew. Erivan Province says the Ottomans held the province 'by 1583'. Date variants: English Wikipedia's 'Kars' and the war article give 1585 for Kars, which conflicts with the 1579 rebuilding attested in the castle and mosque records. Battle of Cildir: 9 August 1578 in the Wikipedia articles, sometimes given as 10 August.
claims.sources: English Wikipedia 'Castle of Kars', 'Kars', 'Peace of Amasya', 'Erivan Province (Safavid Iran)', 'Erivan Fortress' (built 1582-83 by Ferhad Pasha), 'Gyumri'; Turkish Wikipedia 'Revan'in Zapti', 'Kars'; Lynch I (1901) on Kars works under Murad III

claims.quote: Kumayri — today's Gyumri
claims.finding: Kumayri is the old Armenian name. Ghevond records it as a village in the 8th century. Later forms were Kumri, Gumri and Turkish Gumru. It was renamed Alexandropol in 1837, Leninakan in 1924, and Gyumri in 1992. The long dash must go.
claims.sources: Armenian Wikipedia 'Kumayri (berdavan)'; English Wikipedia 'Gyumri'; Lynch I (1901) 'At Alexandropol'

claims.quote: The people endured by their tuff-stone walls and their stubbornness
claims.finding: I found no source on local Armenian resistance in Shirak between 1578 and 1605. Lynch says Gumri was still 'an insignificant village' at the start of the 19th century. The tuff-stone town is 19th-century Alexandropol, so the image is also anachronistic. Removed.
claims.sources: Lynch, Armenia I (1901), ch. 'At Alexandropol'; English and Armenian Wikipedia 'Gyumri'

claims.quote: until Shah Abbas's deportations of 1604 emptied whole valleys
claims.finding: The core fact holds. In autumn 1604 Abbas was besieging Kars when Cigalazade Sinan Pasha approached. He fell back, laid the land waste and deported its people. The removals went on into 1605 (Armenian Wikipedia dates the Nakhchivan phase to 11 August 1605). Lynch says the deportees came from the Araxes valley. Shirak was affected too: Deacon Zakaria of Kanaker (17th c.) lists 'Shirak, Nig, Yeghegnadzor, Gegham, Lori... the Ararat plain, Erevan' among the lands emptied, and Armenian Wikipedia says 'from Shirak to Goghtn'. Totals of 250,000 to 300,000 are chronicle-based estimates and should not be stated as fact. Rewritten with the date as 'from 1604' and the Shirak claim attributed to Zakaria.
claims.sources: Armenian Wikipedia 'Deportation of the Armenian population of Nakhchivan (1605)' (quoting Zakaria Kanakertsi and Arakel of Tabriz) and 'Abbas I'; English Wikipedia 'Iranian Armenia (1502-1828)', 'Erivan Province (Safavid Iran)'; Lynch I (1901) on the Araxes valley deportation

claims.quote: Hold the winter road, and spare Shirak that fate a while longer.
claims.finding: Shirak was in fact hit by the deportation, but the deporter was the Safavid shah, not the Ottoman enemy the player fights in 1579. 'Spare that fate a while longer' links the two in a way that is wrong. Changed to a plain rally line that keeps 'Hold the winter road'.

claims.quote: The stone city beneath snowbound Aragats.
claims.finding: In 1579 there was no stone city. Gumri was a village until the Russian fortress and town of 1837-1840, and the tuff-stone city belongs to the 19th century. 'Beneath Aragats' is fine: the Shirak plateau is bounded by the northern and western foothills of the Aragats massif, and Lynch calls Alagoz the barrier between Alexandropol and the Araxes.

No fighting at Kumayri that year is recorded, and eastern Shirak stayed Safavid until 1583. revised.tag: The frontier plain beneath snowbound Aragats.

rosterFit:
Overall the roster fits an Ottoman frontier army of 1578-1590.
- Azap Skirmishers: fits. Azebs were light infantry and archers levied under Suleiman's kanunname, and fortress azebs made up most of the small garrisons.
- Janissaries / Janissary Guard: fits. Lala Mustafa set out with the kapikulu household troops in April 1578. By the 16th century janissaries were mainly musketeers, so the 'spearman' role is a gameplay label only.
- Sipahi Cavalry: fits. Timariot sipahis made up most of the army, and the provincial contingents joined at Erzurum.
- Great Bombard: acceptable but loose. Ottoman guns are recorded at the frontier fortresses (50 sahi guns at Erivan in 1583), but 'bombard' suggests 15th-century giant siege guns. No change needed.
- Imperial Falcons: invented. The court had falconers but no combat flyers; acceptable as a game abstraction.
- Boss 'The Sultan's Champion': generic and not historical. For 1579 at the Kars/Shirak frontier the right figure is Lala Mustafa Pasha, the serdar of the 1578 campaign, who came to Kars on Murad III's order and rebuilt it in 1579 (he died 7 August 1580). Ozdemiroglu Osman Pasha is wrong here: he was holding Shirvan and Daghestan. If the date moves to 1583, the boss should be Ferhad Pasha.
