target: Era-wide enemy rosters, era names/periods/stories, and global tower/spell/hero names (plus victory text)

claims.quote: Sargon's armies march north across the highlands toward the fortress of Tushpa on the shore of Lake Van.
claims.finding: Sargon II's 714 BC campaign left Nimrud in July 714 and went up the Zab valleys to Lake Urmia. He beat Rusa I there, chased the Urartians west of the lake, and on the way home sacked Musasir, the holy city of Haldi. No attack on Tushpa is recorded, and the campaign had to end before the October snows. The Assyrian army that did reach Tushpa belonged to Tiglath-pileser III, who chased Sarduri II back to the capital in 743 BC. The era also contains Erebuni, 782 BC, decades before Sargon (r. 722-705).
claims.sources: Sargon II, Great Display Inscription of Khorsabad, lines 27-29 (Oppert transl., in Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 1901, PG 10887); Wikipedia (June 2023 dump): Sargon II, Tiglath-Pileser III, Tushpa, Rusa I

claims.quote: Kingdom of Urartu, 8th century BC.
claims.finding: Urartu (native name Biainili) was at its height in the 8th c. BC under Argishti I (c. 785-760), Sarduri II and Rusa I (c. 735-714). Argishti I founded Erebuni in 782 BC.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Urartu, Erebuni Fortress, Tushpa, Rusa I

claims.quote: Cimmerian Raiders
claims.finding: Between 720 and 714 BC, Assyrian intelligence reports from crown prince Sennacherib to Sargon say the Cimmerians attacked Urartu and heavily defeated Rusa I's army. They were Urartu's enemies acting on their own, not Assyrian troops. Assyrian light infantry was mostly Aramean tribesmen armed with bows or spears.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Cimmerians; Sargon II (Urartu-Assyria war, 715 Cimmerian defeat); Neo-Assyrian Empire (army organisation)

claims.quote: Median Cavalry
claims.finding: Sargon's own inscription says he occupied 34 Median towns and 'levied annual tributes of horses upon them'. In 714 his Median vassals supplied his army with provisions and water. I found no Median cavalry unit in his army. Assyria had its own standing cavalry (horse archers and lancers), and it is even recorded using foreign cavalry from Urartu.
claims.sources: Khorsabad Great Inscription line 23 (Oppert transl., 1901); Wikipedia: Sargon II, Medes, Neo-Assyrian Empire; Sayce, Assyria: Its Princes, Priests and People (1885) ch. on army

claims.quote: War Falcons
claims.finding: No use of falcons in war is attested. A relief from Sargon II's palace at Khorsabad was once said to show falconry; read closely, it shows an archer shooting at birds of prey and an attendant catching one. How early falconry began in Mesopotamia is disputed.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Falconry (history and timeline, citing Layard 1853)

claims.quote: Sargon, King of Assyria
claims.finding: Correct for the 714 BC war: Sargon II led it himself and charged with his bodyguard near Lake Urmia. It is wrong for the Erebuni 782 BC battlefield. Shalmaneser IV was king then, and his commander-in-chief (turtanu) Shamshi-ilu campaigned against Argishti I around 780 BC. No Assyrian attack on Erebuni itself is recorded.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Sargon II, Shamshi-ilu, Urartu

claims.quote: Assyrian Spearmen / Assyrian Shieldbearers / Siege Ram
claims.finding: Neo-Assyrian infantry included spearmen with round shields and close-order heavy infantry. Battering rams with one or two spear-like heads were standard siege equipment.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Neo-Assyrian Empire; Sayce, Assyria (1885)

claims.quote: 451 AD — Avarayr
claims.finding: The date is right: Avarayr was fought in 451 (Wikipedia gives 2 June 451; another reckoning gives 26 May). The em dash breaks the house style; use '451 AD, Avarayr'.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Battle of Avarayr (cites Elishe, transl. Thomson 1982)

claims.quote: The Sasanian shahanshah sends the Savaran and his war elephants to bend Armenia's faith.
claims.finding: In 449 Yazdegerd II issued an edict imposing Zoroastrianism on Armenia, and the Persian army at Avarayr included war elephants and savaran cavalry. 'Sends' is right: the shahanshah was not in the field himself.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Vardan Mamikonian, Yazdegerd II, Battle of Avarayr, Mushkan Niusalavurt

claims.quote: Hold the line as Vardan held it at Avarayr.
claims.finding: The Persians won the battle and Vardan was killed along with eight of his top officers. Resistance went on under Vahan Mamikonian until the Treaty of Nvarsak (484) guaranteed religious freedom. Vardan did not hold the line; he stood and fell. Suggested line: 'Stand as Vardan stood at Avarayr.'
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Battle of Avarayr, Mushkan Niusalavurt (Elishe and Lazar Parpetsi as reported)

claims.quote: Immortal Spearmen
claims.finding: 'Immortals' is a Greek name that Procopius and Malalas give to an elite Sasanian CAVALRY unit. Armenian sources on Avarayr mention an elite unit (gund matean), but none of these are spearmen. The Sasanian infantry who carried spears were the paygan: conscript levies with short spears and wicker shields.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Immortals (Sasanian Empire), Paygan, Military of the Sasanian Empire

claims.quote: Savaran Shieldbearers
claims.finding: Aswaran or savaran means 'horsemen': the armoured noble cavalry that was the backbone of the Sasanian army. It cannot name a foot unit of shieldbearers.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Aswaran (etymology from Old Persian asabara)

claims.quote: Yazdegerd II
claims.finding: The minister Mihr-Narseh put Mushkan Niusalavurt in command of the Iranian forces. Mushkan fought at Avarayr in 451 and was badly wounded. No source I consulted places Yazdegerd II on the field.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Mushkan Niusalavurt, Mihr-Narseh, Yazdegerd II

claims.quote: Simurgh Fledglings
claims.finding: The simurgh is a benevolent mythical bird of Persian myth and literature, not an army unit.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Simurgh

claims.quote: Cataphracts / War Elephant / Persian Skirmishers
claims.finding: The Sasanian army had heavy cataphract and clibanarii cavalry, an elephant corps and light horse archers. Elephants are reported at Avarayr.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Military of the Sasanian Empire, Battle of Avarayr

claims.quote: Arab Invasion / 7th century AD
claims.finding: The era also holds battles in 910 and 921 fought against the Sajids. They were an Iranian (Sogdian) dynasty from Ushrusana who ruled Azerbaijan from 889/890 to 929, nominally as governors (ostikans) for the Abbasid caliph. They were neither Arab nor 7th century. Suggested: 'Caliphate Invasion', 7th to 10th century AD.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Sajid dynasty, Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, Smbat I of Armenia ('the Abbasid caliph, Yusuf's nominal sovereign'), Ostikan

claims.quote: The armies of the Caliphate sweep up from the south, and the naxarar lords look to your towers.
claims.finding: This is true for 640. Arab sources have Iyad ibn Ghanm's 639/640 expedition coming up from Upper Mesopotamia as far as Bitlis. Sebeos and Catholicos John V date the sack of Dvin to 640, while other Armenian accounts date it to 642 and Arab sources merge everything into 645/646. 'Naxarar' is the correct term for the Armenian lords. The 10th-century Sajid attacks came from Azerbaijan in the east, so the line covers only part of the era.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Muslim conquest of Armenia, Dvin (ancient city), Theodore Rshtuni

claims.quote: Camel Riders
claims.finding: Early Muslim cavalry used camels for transport, and as food on long marches, but fought on horseback. I found no camel-mounted fighting in the Armenian highlands, and the 10th-century Sajid armies were horse armies.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Rashidun Caliphate (military), Sajid dynasty

claims.quote: Desert Skirmishers / Desert Hawks
claims.finding: These wars were fought in the highlands, and the 10th-century enemy marched from Azerbaijan, not from any desert. Falconry was central to Arab court culture, and the saker is the traditional falconry bird of West Asia, so 'Saker Falcons' is accurate without the desert framing.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Falconry, Sajid dynasty

claims.quote: The Caliph's General
claims.finding: Loosely right for 640. From 909 to 914 the enemy was Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, Sajid emir and ostikan of Arminiya, who had Smbat I tortured to death in 914. At Sevan (921) the opposing commander was Beshir, according to the account based on Draskhanakerttsi. Acceptable as an era-wide fallback; better replaced per battlefield.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, Smbat I of Armenia, Battle of Sevan, Hovhannes Draskhanakerttsi

claims.quote: Old stone against new gunpowder.
claims.finding: Gunpowder was not new in 1579. The Janissaries began adopting firearms in the 1440s, and Ottoman heavy artillery decided Chaldiran against the Safavids in 1514, 65 years before the Gyumri Road battle.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Janissary (equipment), Battle of Chaldiran

claims.quote: Janissaries drill in the valley and the Sultan's great bombards roll up the mountain road.
claims.finding: Broadly acceptable. The Ottomans invaded Safavid-held Erivan province in 1578 and held it by 1583, and their artillery was well established. 'Great bombard' calls up the giant 15th-century guns (the Dardanelles Gun of 1464), so 'siege guns' is safer. Sultan Murad III never went on campaign, but the guns were his.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Erivan Province (Safavid Iran), Bombard (weapon), Murad III

claims.quote: Janissaries (spearman role)
claims.finding: By the early 16th century the Janissaries were trained musketeers. Separately, the game's wave banner takes the first word of the spearman name, so it currently reads 'Janissaries forces advance'.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Janissary; game source index.html lines 2478 and 24511

claims.quote: The Sultan's Champion
claims.finding: Murad III never went on campaign. Lala Mustafa Pasha commanded the 1578 Caucasus campaign, won at Cildir on 9 August 1578, and rebuilt Kars fortress in 1579.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Murad III, Lala Mustafa Pasha, Lala Mustafa Pasha's Caucasian campaign, Battle of Cildir, Castle of Kars

claims.quote: Azap Skirmishers / Sipahi Cavalry / Janissary Guard / Imperial Falcons
claims.finding: Azebs were irregular infantry archers who fought in front of the cannon and Janissaries. Timariot sipahis made up most of the army. The Ottoman court kept falconers: a chief falconer (dogancibasi), a cakircibasi, and Ibrahim as Suleiman's royal falconer.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Azeb, Sipahi, List of Ottoman titles (Chakirji), Suleiman the Magnificent, Telli Hasan Pasha, Piali Pasha

claims.quote: Ballista / Catapult (towers shown in every era)
claims.finding: The earliest ballista is thought to have been built for Dionysius of Syracuse around 400 BC, so it and any torsion catapult are three centuries too late for Urartu. Traction trebuchets (mangonels) were adopted by the Byzantines around 587, the Persians in the early 7th century and the Arabs in the later 7th, and they largely replaced torsion artillery from then on. In 1579 the real equivalents were cannon.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Ballista, Trebuchet, Mangonel, Abbasid Caliphate (military); Ammianus Marcellinus 19.7.6-7 (ballistae on Amida's towers, 359)

claims.quote: Fire Altar (Christian Armenian defender tower in 451 and later)
claims.finding: The fire altar was the Zoroastrian emblem on Yazdegerd II's coins. The 451 war was fought against his 449 edict imposing Zoroastrianism, so a Christian Armenian fire altar inverts the conflict.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Yazdegerd II (coinage), Vardan Mamikonian, Mihr-Narseh

claims.quote: Wrath of Haldi / Standards of Haldi (all eras)
claims.finding: Haldi was Urartu's chief god: his cult was introduced under Ishpuini, and Sargon carried his statue off from Musasir in 714. Armenia had been Christian since 301, so Haldi names fit only era 0.
claims.sources: Khorsabad Great Inscription lines 28-29 (Oppert transl.); Wikipedia: Urartu, Battle of Avarayr

claims.quote: Longbow Corps
claims.finding: The armies of all four eras used composite bows: the Assyrians adopted them, and the Ottomans used composite-bow archers until Lepanto in 1571. 'Longbow' suggests the English war bow.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Composite bow

claims.quote: Vardan the Defender (hero, all eras)
claims.finding: Vardan Mamikonian died at Avarayr in 451. He cannot fight in 782 BC, 714 BC, 640, 910, 921 or 1579.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Vardan Mamikonian, Battle of Avarayr

claims.quote: The kochari is danced before the gates
claims.finding: Kochari is a folk circle dance of the Armenian highlands, also danced in variant forms by Assyrians, Azerbaijanis, Kurds and Pontic Greeks. UNESCO inscribed the Armenian form in 2017 and the Azerbaijani Yalli forms in 2018. Wikipedia's 'over a thousand years' is unsourced, and I found no ancient or medieval attestation. Wikipedia even says it spread to eastern Armenia only after 1915. So it does not fit 782 BC, 714 BC or 451, and is unproven for any era here.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Kochari, Armenian dance

claims.quote: Frost of Aragats / Rain of Arrows
claims.finding: Aragats is a real Armenian mountain inside Urartian and later Armenian territory, and mass archery fits every era. Neither name makes a historical claim that needs changing.
claims.sources: Wikipedia: Urartu (Aras and Sevan territories), Military of the Sasanian Empire (arrow storms)

revised.name: Caliphate Invasion
revised.history: 640 to 921 AD. In 640, the chroniclers record, the armies of the Caliphate swept up from the south and sacked Dvin; Sebeos counts 35,000 captives. For nearly two centuries the Caliph's governors ruled from Dvin. Then the Bagratids won back a crown, and the Sajid emirs of Azerbaijan, ruling in the Caliph's name, came for it: Yusuf put King Smbat I to death in 914, and his son Ashot II fought on. The naxarar lords look to your towers. Do not let the highlands break.

(b) Desert Skirmishers becomes Caliphate Raiders.

The Ashot II article also places a Sevan victory in 927/8, so the 921 date has a variant. In 921 Yusuf himself may have been in caliphal captivity; that is unverified here, low confidence.
